beats.headline: Why ditch the synchronized keyword?
beats.subline: Synchronized blocks are rigid. They lack timeouts, interrupts, and granular control.
beats.narration: Synchronized blocks are the default, but they're rigid. You cannot set timeouts, you cannot interrupt them, and they share one wait set. Let's look at the alternatives.

beats.title: ReentrantLock with Conditions

steps.explanation: Allows the thread to respond to interrupts, preventing permanent hangs.
Mandatory. If you forget this, you leak the lock forever.

beats.narration: Always use lockInterruptibly and wrap the critical section in a finally block. Unlike synchronized, the JVM won't clean up your lock if an exception escapes.

beats.title: ReadWriteLock vs. Standard Lock
beats.narration: If your state is read-heavy, ReentrantLock is a bottleneck. ReadWriteLock lets multiple readers in simultaneously, only locking exclusively for writers.

beats.title: StampedLock Optimistic Reads
beats.caption: No lock acquisition for hot paths
beats.narration: StampedLock is the speed king. Optimistic reads grab a version stamp without locking. If the data hasn't changed, you're done. No lock overhead at all.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Atomic variables and the CAS loop →
beats.narration: That's the locking layer. In Part 2, we dive into lock-free atomic variables and how CAS instructions keep your counters fast.

beats.headline: Locks are slow. Can we do better?
beats.subline: Hardware-level Compare-And-Swap (CAS) lets you update state without ever blocking a thread.
beats.narration: Locks are pessimistic. They assume conflict and block. Atomics are optimistic. They use CPU-level CAS instructions to update state without ever stopping a thread.

beats.title: The CAS Retry Loop

steps.explanation: The retry loop is essential because CAS might fail if another thread wins.
Atomic hardware instruction: update only if value is still 'current'.

beats.narration: The CAS loop is the heart of lock-free code. You read, you check, and you attempt to swap. If another thread beat you to it, you simply retry.

beats.title: AtomicLong vs LongAdder

nodes.label: LongAdder
nodes.detail: Striped cells, padded to avoid cache-line bouncing

beats.narration: AtomicLong hits a wall under high contention because every core fights for the same cache line. LongAdder stripes the work across multiple cells to scale linearly.

beats.title: The ABA Problem

steps.explanation: Pairs the value with a version stamp to prevent ABA bugs.

beats.narration: The ABA problem happens when a value changes from A to B and back to A. CAS thinks nothing changed. AtomicStampedReference fixes this by tracking a version stamp.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.narration: Atomics are fast, but complex. In Part 3, we simplify your life with concurrent collections that handle the heavy lifting for you.

beats.headline: Stop wrapping collections in synchronized!
beats.subline: Coarse locking kills performance. Use concurrent-specific structures designed for multi-core scaling.
beats.narration: Wrapping a map in synchronized is a performance killer. It serializes everything. Concurrent collections are designed for lock-free reads and granular bucket locking.

beats.title: ConcurrentHashMap Internals

nodes.label: Writes
nodes.detail: Locking only on the specific bucket head

beats.narration: ConcurrentHashMap is a masterpiece. Reads are lock-free. Writes only lock the specific bucket head. And if collisions spike, it converts linked lists into red-black trees.

beats.title: Check-Then-Act Bugs
beats.narration: Never combine two map calls. Two threads can check and then both put. Use computeIfAbsent to make the check and insertion a single atomic operation.

beats.title: CopyOnWriteArrayList

steps.explanation: Every mutation creates a new array. Perfect for read-heavy listener lists.

beats.narration: CopyOnWriteArrayList is for lists you read constantly but change rarely. Iterators work on a snapshot, so you never get a concurrent modification exception.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.narration: Collections are sorted. In Part 4, we use BlockingQueues to build robust producer-consumer pipelines without managing raw threads.

beats.headline: Stop writing your own wait/notify loops.
beats.subline: BlockingQueues handle backpressure, locking, and thread handoffs out of the box.
beats.narration: Stop writing manual wait-notify loops. BlockingQueues handle the queueing, locking, and backpressure for you. It's the standard for producer-consumer pipelines.

beats.title: Queue Method Families
beats.narration: Choose your method family. Use exceptions for strict logic, special values for non-blocking checks, or blocking methods to apply natural backpressure.

beats.title: Producer-Consumer Pipeline

steps.explanation: Efficiently parks the thread until data arrives.

beats.narration: ArrayBlockingQueue is your best friend for backpressure. If the queue is full, the producer blocks. If it's empty, the consumer waits. Simple, robust, and fast.

beats.title: Queue Implementations
beats.narration: LinkedBlockingQueue uses separate locks for put and take, scaling better than array versions. Use SynchronousQueue if you need a direct handoff with zero buffering.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
beats.narration: Queues are ready. In Part 5, we wrap up with Synchronizers: CountDownLatches, Barriers, and Semaphores for complex thread coordination.

beats.headline: How do you sync 100 threads?
beats.subline: CountDownLatches, Barriers, and Semaphores are the final pieces of the concurrency puzzle.
beats.narration: Coordinating multiple threads is hard. Synchronizers make it easy. From one-shot gates to reusable barriers, here is how you manage complex thread lifecycles.

beats.title: Choosing a Synchronizer

nodes.label: Latch
nodes.detail: One-shot gate, wait for N tasks

beats.narration: Use a Latch for startup gates. Use a Barrier for multi-phase parallel algorithms. Use a Semaphore to cap access to scarce resources like database connections.

beats.title: Rate Limiting with Semaphores

steps.explanation: Limits concurrent outbound calls to exactly 20.
Always release in finally to prevent resource starvation.

beats.narration: Semaphores are perfect for rate limiting. Acquire a permit before calling an external API and release it in a finally block. It's the cleanest way to cap concurrency.

beats.title: Concurrency Cheat Sheet
beats.caption: Your toolkit for high-performance Java
beats.narration: That's the package. Locks for safety, Atomics for speed, Collections for data, and Synchronizers for coordination. Master these, and you've mastered Java concurrency.
